slides.title: Room 1: Money
slides.narration: Welcome to Lesson 6. From here on, we walk through nine rooms: the subjects that shape daily married life. We begin with money.

slides.quote: “Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, for riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations?”
slides.narration:
Let’s start with Scripture. Proverbs chapter 27, verses 23 and 24.

“Know well the condition of your flocks, and give attention to your herds, for riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations?”

slides.title: Know. Give attention. Do not assume.
body: A proverb from a farming world: know well the condition of what you have. The wisdom is attention and honesty about what is actually there.
slides.narration:
This is a proverb from a farming world, where a household’s livelihood was kept in its flocks and herds. The advice is very practical: know well the condition of what you have. Give it your attention. Do not assume.

And notice the reason. “Riches do not last forever; and does a crown endure to all generations?” Nothing material is permanent, not even a crown. So a wise person does not drift along assuming all is well. The wise person looks.

Notice, too, what the proverb does not say. It does not say, “Become wealthy.” It says, “Know.” The wisdom here is attention and honesty about what is actually there.

slides.title: Count the cost
body: Jesus describes a man building a tower who first sits down to count the cost. We borrow only the simple wisdom: honest counting before costly commitment.
slides.narration: Jesus makes a similar ordinary point in Luke 14:28, though his subject is different. He is speaking to crowds about the cost of following him, not about household budgets. He uses the picture of a man building a tower, who first sits down and counts the cost, to see whether he has enough to finish. We borrow only the simple wisdom in the picture, and we leave the passage’s own meaning intact: honest counting should come before costly commitment.

slides.title: Know what you have and what you owe
body: Faithful stewardship begins there. Engagement is the season for counting.
slides.narration: Here is the truth this lesson stands on. Faithful stewardship begins with knowing what you actually have and what you actually owe. And engagement is the season for counting.

slides.title: Money touches
slides.narration: Money is one of the places where this matters most, and it is rarely only about money. Notice how it can touch trust, because you have to be honest about what you have and owe. It can touch stewardship, because what we have has been entrusted to us. It can touch generosity, because what we give shows something of what we value. And it can touch shame, which is why so many people avoid it.

slides.title: Transparency before agreement
body: Marriage requires financial transparency before it requires financial agreement.
slides.sub: You do not need identical habits. You do need to know what you are marrying into.
slides.narration: So the principle for this room is: marriage requires financial transparency before it requires financial agreement. You do not need identical habits. You do need to know what you are marrying into.

slides.title: “Why didn’t you tell me?”
body: “Because I knew you’d react like this.”
slides.sub: Ask the question without humiliation. Fear of a reaction does not excuse concealment.
slides.narration:
Here is what usually goes wrong.

One partner discovers significant debt that the other never mentioned. The conversation begins: “Why didn’t you tell me?” And the answer comes: “Because I knew you’d react like this.” “So you’ve been hiding things from me?”

Notice that the question “Why didn’t you tell me?” is legitimate. Ask it without humiliation. But do not use fear of the reaction to excuse concealment. You may even need two conversations, one about the facts and one about the breach of trust.

slides.title: Income, but not behaviour
body: They know each other’s salaries. They have never talked about spending, debt, giving, saving, or what is reasonable to spend without asking.
slides.narration:
Three other failures are common.

The first is talking about income but not behaviour. They know each other’s salaries. They have never talked about spending habits, debt, what each sends to family, giving, saving, or what counts as a reasonable amount to spend without asking. So they say “we’ll be fine” while picturing two completely different lifestyles.

slides.title: Privacy and disclosure
body: Keep your financial independence before marriage. But debts, commitments and risks that materially affect your shared life need to be disclosed.
slides.sub: A demand for control is not the same as a request for honesty.
slides.narration: The second is about privacy and disclosure. Each of you keeps your financial independence before marriage. But debts, commitments and risks that materially affect your shared life need to be disclosed. Transparency does not require surrendering passwords, merging accounts during your engagement, or accepting surveillance. A demand for control is not the same as a request for honesty.

slides.title: Income used as authority
body: “I pay for most of this, so I should have more say.” Now money has become about worth and control.
slides.narration: The third is income used as authority. The higher earner begins to think, without ever saying it, “I pay for most of this, so I should have more say.” The lower earner becomes defensive, or dependent, or quietly ashamed. And now money has become about worth and control.

slides.title: What does money make you feel that you have not told anyone?
body: Take a moment before you go on.
slides.narration: Pause here. What does money make you feel that you have not told anyone? Take a moment before you go on.

slides.title: Disclose first
body: Everything that materially affects the life you are building. Real numbers, not vague reassurance.
slides.narration:
So what do couples who do this well actually do?

They disclose everything that materially affects the life they are considering building together, before they negotiate anything. Real numbers, not vague reassurance. Income. All debt. Savings. Fixed monthly costs. What they send to family. What they give. What they hope to buy or build. They do not wait until after the wedding for one of them to discover that the other sends a substantial amount home every month.

slides.title: What does spending mean to you?
body: Not “you’re terrible with money,” but “what do you normally spend money on, and what does spending it mean to you?”
slides.narration: They discuss habits without shaming. Not “you’re terrible with money,” but “what do you normally spend money on, and what does spending it mean to you?” That second question opens something the first one closes. One may save because money means safety: “I grew up with very little, and savings are the only thing that makes me feel secure.” The other spends on experiences because “money is for making memories with the people I love.” Those meanings help explain the disagreement. You still need to check what is affordable.

slides.title: With a number attached
body: Not “we’ll be careful.” And be willing to say: “There’s something about my finances I’m embarrassed about, and you need to know it before we marry.”
slides.narration:
They turn good intentions into clear agreements. Not “we’ll be careful,” but something specific, with a number attached.

And they are willing to say, “There’s something about my finances I’m embarrassed about, and you need to know it before we marry.” That sentence costs something. It is worth more than every impressive thing you could say about your money.

body: “Thank you for telling me. I need to understand the facts, and what this means for trust, before we decide our next step.”
slides.sub: You are allowed to be hurt, to ask questions and to take time.
slides.narration: When someone says it to you, you might answer: “Thank you for telling me. I need to understand the facts, and what this means for trust, before we decide our next step.” You are allowed to be hurt. You are allowed to ask questions and take time. And a single imperfect response does not decide whether honesty will ever be possible again.

slides.title: What kind is it?
list: Different habits: workable, with specific rules you both keep.
Different obligations: name the actual figure and expectation. Do not settle it in one evening.
Significant undisclosed debt: it changes the information you are deciding on.
slides.narration: When you find a real difference, ask what kind it is. Different habits, one saves and one spends, are workable, with specific rules that you both keep. Different obligations, where one of you supports family and the other does not, is one of the most common serious differences, and it is rarely just about money. It is about duty, culture and what a good son or daughter owes. Do not settle it in one evening. Do name the actual figure and the actual expectation, because the vague version is what causes the damage. There is no single arrangement that suits every couple or every culture. And significant undisclosed debt is more than a difference in financial habits. It changes the information on which you are making your decision, and it may also raise questions about trust. You need to decide together what to do with it. That may take weeks. Take the weeks.

slides.note: If money is being used to control, threaten or trap someone, that is not a budgeting problem. If either of you feels pressured to transfer money, take on debt or give up access to your own funds, pause the exercise and seek independent advice.
slides.narration: One more word, and it is a serious one. If money is being used to control, threaten or trap someone, that is not a budgeting problem. If either of you feels pressured to transfer money, take on debt or give up access to your own funds, pause the exercise and seek independent advice. When you review documents together, cover sensitive numbers such as account numbers and passwords.

slides.title: The Money Snapshot
body: About 30 minutes. Real figures, not comfortable ones.
list: What do I earn, and how stable is it?
What do I owe, all of it?
What are my fixed monthly commitments?
What do I send to family, or expect to?
slides.sub: Mark estimates. Leave out passwords and full account numbers.
slides.narration: Your step has two parts. First, alone, about 30 minutes. Fill in the Money Snapshot from the worksheet. Real figures, not comfortable ones. What do I earn, and how stable is it? What do I owe, all of it? What do I have saved? What are my fixed monthly commitments? What do I send to family, or expect to? Mark estimates as estimates, and leave out passwords and full account numbers.

slides.title: 45 to 60 minutes
body: Exchange the relevant figures and read both in silence before either speaks. Then talk about what money means: what it felt like where you grew up, and when you have felt ashamed about it.
slides.narration: Then, together, 45 to 60 minutes, when neither of you is tired. Have your Lesson 2 rules in front of you. Exchange the relevant figures and read both in silence before either of you speaks. Then talk about what the money means: what money felt like in the house you grew up in, what spending means to you, what saving means to you, and when you have felt ashamed about money.

slides.title: Agree one rule today
body: Joint or separate accounts, spending without asking, giving, what you each owe your families, saving, who pays the bills. Record the rest to revisit.
slides.narration: Then look at the areas in the worksheet: joint or separate accounts, the amount either of you can spend without asking, giving, what you each owe to your families, saving, and who pays the bills and how the other stays informed. You will not settle all of these in this sitting. Agree one rule today, and record the other matters you need to revisit. The First Household Budget can wait for another day.

slides.title: Out loud
body: “Is there anything about my finances I have not told you?”
slides.sub: And wait. Do not fill the silence.
slides.narration:
Then finish with the hard question, out loud: “Is there anything about my finances I have not told you?” And wait. Do not fill the silence.

Before you leave, record the one financial rule you agreed and one matter that still needs checking.

body: If what you wrote differs from what you now want to say, ask: has my thinking changed, or am I afraid to be honest?
slides.narration: Your inventory from Lesson 3 stays yours. Keep it beside you as a reference. If what you had written differs from what you now want to say, pause and ask yourself: has my thinking changed, or am I afraid to be honest? Give an honest answer when it is safe, and ask for time if you need it.

body: Lord, teach us to count the cost honestly. Give us courage to say what we owe and what we fear. Keep us from hiding and from shaming. Help us hold what You have given us with open hands, and with truth between us. Amen.
slides.narration:
Let me close with a short prayer.

Lord, teach us to count the cost honestly. Give us courage to say what we owe and what we fear. Keep us from hiding and from shaming. Help us hold what You have given us with open hands, and with truth between us. Amen.
